explain.say: In 1954, researchers took two groups of 11-year-old boys to a summer camp in Robbers Cave State Park, Oklahoma, USA. At first, neither group knew the other existed. Look at the board. See the happy faces? Each group made friends and chose a name: the Eagles and the Rattlers.

explain.say: Look at the next pictures. Psychologist Muzafer Sherif set up contests between the groups, with prizes only for winners. Soon the rivalry grew: the boys called each other names, burned each other's flag and raided cabins. See the angry face? Why do you think prizes for only one side caused trouble?

explain.say: This shows how quickly people split into "us", the in-group, and "them", the out-group, when they compete for something only one side can win. Just meeting was not enough: shared meals turned into food fights. Have you seen sports fans or classes act like this?

explain.say: Now see shared problem. The researchers set up problems that affected everyone, like a broken water supply, that needed both groups to solve. A goal that both groups need and neither can reach alone is called a superordinate goal. What shared goal could unite two rival teams you know?

explain.say: And the last picture: working together, the boys became friendlier, and some ended up on the same bus home. Today, some researchers question how the study was run and how it was reported, so it is a lesson, not the final word. Well done! Challenge: think of a shared goal that could bring two groups at your school together.

faq.q: What was the Robbers Cave experiment?
faq.a: It was a 1954 study by psychologist Muzafer Sherif and colleagues at a summer camp in Oklahoma. Two groups of boys became rivals when they competed for prizes, and became friendlier when they worked together on shared problems.

faq.q: Who took part in the Robbers Cave experiment?
faq.a: Twenty-two 11-year-old boys from similar backgrounds were split into two groups that did not know about each other at first. They named themselves the Eagles and the Rattlers.
asks: Who were the Eagles and Rattlers?

faq.q: Why did the groups become hostile?
faq.a: They competed for prizes that only one side could win. Competition for scarce rewards turned "us and them" feelings into name-calling and raids. This idea is called realistic conflict theory.
A superordinate goal is a goal that both groups want and can only reach by working together, like fixing a shared water supply. It helps rivals see each other as one team.
asks: How do you unite rival groups?

faq.q: Did working together really end the conflict?
faq.a: In the study, shared goals reduced hostility and built friendships. Later researchers have criticised parts of how Sherif ran and reported his studies, so many treat it as a useful lesson rather than proof.
asks: Tell me about work as one
Is the Robbers Cave study reliable?

facts: Muzafer Sherif and colleagues ran the Robbers Cave study in 1954 with 22 boys aged about 11.
Psychologist Gina Perry's 2018 book "The Lost Boys" questioned aspects of how Sherif's camp studies were run and reported.
